headline: The weed killer weeds learned to beat
dek: In 1970 John Franz found that glyphosate kills weeds. Sold as Roundup, it became the world's most used herbicide, and 62 weed species have evolved to survive it.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: Kill weeds without the plow
slides.text: Farmers controlled weeds by plowing, which costs topsoil, time and fuel. What they wanted was one weed killer that took out tough annual and perennial weeds alike and did not stay active in the soil.

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: Roundup
slides.text: In 1970 Franz, a Monsanto chemist, found that glyphosate did the job. Sold as Roundup from 1974, it controls over 125 kinds of weeds and helped make no-till farming possible. In 1987 he received the National Medal of Technology.

slides.label: Wait, what?
slides.title: The same year
slides.text: In 1996 the first crop engineered to survive glyphosate, a soybean, went on sale in the US. That same year, in an Australian apple orchard, the first weed was found that had evolved to survive glyphosate too.

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: The survivors took over
slides.statLabel: weed species that have evolved resistance to glyphosate, in 31 countries
slides.text: Global use rose almost 15-fold from 1995 to 2014, after those crops arrived, often as the only weed killer on a field. Each spraying left the rare weeds it could not kill. Many resistant weeds now shrug off other herbicides too.
also: Source: Alcántara-de la Cruz and others, Pest Management Science, 2026

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: Doubted, then disputed
slides.text: In 1997 Monsanto scientists wrote that decades of use had produced no verified resistant weeds. On cancer, a WHO agency in 2015 called glyphosate probably carcinogenic. US and EU regulators found it unlikely to be, and the EPA is reviewing it again, due in 2027.

slides.label: Where it stands
slides.title: Still in court, still on shelves
slides.text: Bayer, which owns Monsanto, says glyphosate is safe. In 2020 it agreed to pay up to $10.9 billion over cancer claims, admitting no liability. In 2026 the Supreme Court barred state claims that the label should have warned of cancer, without ruling on the science.

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: Control of over 125 kinds of annual and perennial weeds (National Inventors Hall of Fame)
Weed control with less plowing, saving topsoil, time and fuel (National Inventors Hall of Fame)
A key tool behind no-till farming (Lemelson-MIT)
costs: 62 weed species resistant to it, in 31 countries (Pest Management Science, 2026)
Resistant weeds that often survive other herbicides too
A cancer question still argued, and up to $10.9 billion in settlements (Bayer, 2020)
slides.text: Glyphosate made weeding cheaper and plowing less necessary. Leaning on it everywhere wore down the very thing that made it work. You decide if it was worth it.

slides.label: Credit for trying
slides.title: We owe him one
slides.text: Franz took on a real problem: weeds that cost farmers crops, fuel and soil. His discovery did that job better than almost anything before it. What the rest of us learned is how fast weeds adapt to a tool that is used everywhere.

slides.label: Pattern
slides.title: The cure breeds resistance
slides.why: Backfires repeat. We sort every one into nine patterns, so you can spot one before you make one yourself.

slides.label: How you do this
slides.title: Your filters train the spammers
slides.text: Your team blocks spam by banning a list of words. Most junk stops. The messages that slip through are the ones with clever misspellings, and those senders keep at it. Soon nearly all your spam is misspelled, and the list catches none of it.
also: Lice shampoo that leaves behind the lice it can't kill
Antibiotics stopped early, leaving the toughest germs

slides.label: Lessons
slides.title: What we take from it
items: The more one tool is used, the faster the problem adapts to it.
A long record with no resistance said little about what heavier use would bring.
A safety question can stay open for decades while the product stays on the shelf.
